title: Level 0: Meet the ESP32 Brain
subtitle: Discovering the ESP32 DevKit & C Architecture

conceptByte.title: Computers vs Microcontrollers
conceptByte.metaphor: The Smartphone vs The Reflex Muscle
keyTakeaways: Your laptop or phone is a general-purpose computer. It runs a massive operating system, renders desktop windows, and browses websites, but cannot toggle physical electrical pins at microsecond speed.
The ESP32 DevKit V1 is a microcontroller. It has no screen, no mouse, and no operating system lag. It executes your compiled C code directly on bare silicon.

Under the silver metal shield is the dual-core 32-bit Xtensa LX6 processor running at 240 MHz (240 million calculations per second) with 520 KB SRAM and built-in 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi + Bluetooth. The 30 metal pins along the edges connect your C code directly to the real world.
conceptByte.analogyStory: If your laptop is a massive library with millions of books, the ESP32 is an Olympic sprinter waiting on the starting block. It doesn't waste time loading desktop windows or checking background notifications. It boots up in 5 milliseconds and focuses 100% of its silicon brainpower on executing your C setup() and loop() instructions, reading sensors, and switching electrical pins.

quizGate.question: Which microcontroller board is sitting in your kit on the desk right now?
options: ESP32 DevKit V1 (Black board with 30 pre-soldered header pins, dual push buttons, and a silver ESP-WROOM-32 Wi-Fi shield)
Raspberry Pi Pico (Green board with an RP2040 chip)
Arduino Uno (Big blue board with a bulky USB-B cable)
quizGate.hint: Look for the black board with the ESP-WROOM-32 metal shield and the onboard EN and BOOT buttons.
quizGate.explanation: You are using the ESP32 DevKit V1, powered by the dual-core 32-bit Xtensa LX6 processor at 240 MHz with built-in Wi-Fi and Bluetooth.

quizGate.question: Why do engineers program microcontrollers in C instead of running scripts through a laptop operating system?
options: Laptops are not powerful enough to read temperature
Microcontrollers execute compiled C instructions directly on silicon with zero operating system lag, switching voltages in nanoseconds
Microcontrollers are only used for playing music
quizGate.hint: Laptops have complex operating systems that add unpredictable lag; compiled C connects directly to electrical hardware.
quizGate.explanation: Microcontrollers execute compiled C code directly on bare metal, bridging software logic to real electrical voltages (0V and 3.3V) with deterministic microsecond precision.

circuitSteps.title: Inspect Your ESP32 DevKit V1
circuitSteps.instruction: Gently remove the ESP32 DevKit V1 from its anti-static foam. Notice the micro-USB port at the top, the silver ESP-WROOM-32 metal RF shield, the EN and BOOT tactile buttons, the red power LED, and the 30 pre-soldered header pins.

codeChunks.title: Hardware Inspection Check
codeChunks.explanation: In C, every Arduino/ESP32 program requires two fundamental functions: setup() runs once on boot, and loop() runs repeatedly forever.

verificationChallenge.instruction: Inspect your ESP32 DevKit V1 board. Verify that the 30 pins are straight and the micro-USB port is clean.
verificationChallenge.expectedObservableResult: Your team is ready to connect the USB cable and upload your first C program in Level 1.

title: Level 1: The First Spark in C
subtitle: Blinking the ESP32 Onboard LED (GPIO 2)

conceptByte.title: Digital Output & The Speed of C
keyTakeaways: A Digital Output pin has only two electrical states: HIGH (supplying 3.3 volts of electrical pressure) or LOW (cutting voltage to 0 volts / Ground).
In C, you configure pin directions in setup() using pinMode(2, OUTPUT). Then in loop(), you use digitalWrite(2, HIGH) to turn it ON and digitalWrite(2, LOW) to turn it OFF.

The ESP32 executes over 240 million clock cycles every second! If you don't pause with delay(500), the LED toggles millions of times a second and looks permanently frozen on. We pause with delay(500) so human eyes can see the blink!
conceptByte.analogyStory: Imagine holding a flashlight switch. Flicking it up turns the bulb on; flicking it down turns it off. The ESP32 processor can flick that switch millions of times every single second. Without delay(500) to pause execution, human eyes only perceive a continuous blur. We pause so our human visual system can keep up with the speed of silicon!

quizGate.question: What does a Digital Output pin do when you call digitalWrite(2, HIGH) in C?
options: It plays a loud sound through the computer speaker
It connects the pin to 3.3 volts of electrical potential
It shuts down the ESP32 to save battery
quizGate.hint: HIGH means electrical 1, which supplies the operating voltage of 3.3V.
quizGate.explanation: Calling digitalWrite(pin, HIGH) connects the internal transistor to 3.3 volts. Calling digitalWrite(pin, LOW) connects it to 0 volts (Ground).

quizGate.question: Why is delay(500) necessary inside the C loop() function?
options: Without delay, the ESP32 toggles the pin millions of times a second, making the LED appear solid to human eyes
The ESP32 runs out of memory if it does not rest
C requires delay commands to compile the binary
quizGate.hint: Microcontrollers think in nanoseconds; human persistence of vision needs half a second to register changes.
quizGate.explanation: Without delay(), the LED toggles at megahertz frequencies. Human eyes see an average glow rather than distinct pulses.

circuitSteps.title: Connect the Micro-USB Cable
circuitSteps.instruction: Plug the micro-USB cable into the ESP32 DevKit V1. Plug the other end into your laptop. If your laptop only has USB-C ports, use the USB-C adapter from your kit.

codeChunks.title: Step 1: Declare Constant Pin Variable
codeChunks.code: const int ONBOARD_LED = 2; // Built-in blue LED on ESP32 GPIO 2
codeChunks.explanation: On the ESP32 DevKit V1, the built-in blue surface-mount LED is hardwired to GPIO 2.

codeChunks.title: Step 2: Configure Pin in setup()
codeChunks.explanation: setup() runs once when the board powers on. pinMode(2, OUTPUT) enables the pin's output driver.

codeChunks.title: Step 3: The Infinite Blink loop()
codeChunks.explanation: loop() executes continuously forever, cycling the LED ON and OFF every half second.

verificationChallenge.instruction: Upload the code to your ESP32. Look directly at the board next to the silver shield: the built-in blue LED should pulse steadily once every second.
verificationChallenge.expectedObservableResult: A crisp, bright blue surface-mount LED on the ESP32 PCB flashing on and off steadily once per second.

title: Level 2: Building on the Breadboard
subtitle: LED Anatomy, Current-Limiting Resistors & ESP32 GPIO in C

conceptByte.title: LED Anatomy, Resistors & Breadboards
conceptByte.metaphor: The One-Way Gate, The Water Valve & The Subway Clips
keyTakeaways: Inside an LED: LED stands for Light Emitting Diode. It is a one-way street for electricity! The longer metal lead is the Anode (+). The shorter lead and the flat edge on the plastic casing rim mark the Cathode (-). If you wire it backwards, zero current flows and it stays dark.

The Resistor (Current Limiter): An LED has almost zero resistance once lit. If you connect it directly across 3.3V, a massive rush of current will burn out the tiny semiconductor die and damage the ESP32 pin! A 220 ohm resistor acts like a water valve, restricting current to a safe 15 milliamps.

Under the Breadboard: The white plastic breadboard is full of springy metal clips underneath. Groups of 5 holes (A-B-C-D-E) are joined together sideways. The outer blue (-) and red (+) strips run continuously all the way down the board to distribute power and Ground.
conceptByte.analogyStory: Think of electrical current like high-pressure water rushing through a pipe. An LED is a fragile decorative water wheel that only spins in one direction. The 220 ohm resistor is a safety nozzle that restricts the rushing water to a gentle stream. Without the resistor nozzle, the water pressure blows the wheel right off its hinges!

quizGate.question: How can you reliably identify the positive leg (Anode) of an LED with your eyes?
options: It is the longer metal lead (while the shorter lead and flat edge on the casing rim mark the Cathode)
It is the shorter metal lead near the flat edge of the casing
Both legs are identical; direction does not matter
quizGate.hint: Remember: The longer lead is the Anode (+); the shorter lead and the flat edge on the casing rim mark the Cathode (-).
quizGate.explanation: The longer lead is the Anode (+) and connects to 3.3V power or GPIO. The shorter lead and the flat edge on the casing rim mark the Cathode (-), connecting to Ground.

quizGate.question: What happens if you connect an LED directly to an ESP32 GPIO pin without a 220 ohm resistor?
options: The light turns blue
Too much current rushes through the semiconductor, overheating and permanently destroying the LED and risking the ESP32 GPIO pin
The ESP32 increases its Wi-Fi speed
quizGate.hint: The resistor limits the flow of electric current.
quizGate.explanation: Without a current-limiting resistor, excessive current flows, burning out the LED diode and risking damage to the ESP32 GPIO driver.

circuitSteps.title: Connect ESP32 Ground to Blue Rail (-)
circuitSteps.instruction: Plug a black jumper wire from ESP32 GND (Pin 14 or Pin 17) into the long Blue Ground Rail (-) on the breadboard. This establishes your 0V reference line.

circuitSteps.title: Extend Ground into Circuit Area (Row 18)
circuitSteps.instruction: Plug a black jumper wire from the Blue Ground Rail (-) into Breadboard Row 18, Column F on the right side of the board. This delivers Ground directly to your LED's cathode row.

circuitSteps.title: Connect ESP32 GPIO 15 (D15) to Row 15
circuitSteps.instruction: Plug a green jumper wire from ESP32 D15 (GPIO 15) into Breadboard Row 15, Column B on the left side of the board. This brings the 3.3V control signal to this row.

circuitSteps.title: Bridge 220Ω Resistor Across the Trench
circuitSteps.instruction: Insert one leg of the 220 ohm resistor (Red-Red-Brown-Gold) into Row 15, Column E, and bridge it across the central trough into Row 15, Column F on the other side of the board.

circuitSteps.title: Insert 5mm Green LED (Anode & Cathode)
circuitSteps.instruction: Insert the longer leg (Anode +) into Row 15, Column H (connected to the resistor). Insert the shorter leg with the flat rim notch (Cathode -) into Row 18, Column H (connected to Ground).
circuitSteps.polarityNote: Anode (+) in Row 15 Col H (from Resistor); Cathode (-) with flat rim in Row 18 Col H (to Ground)

codeChunks.title: Step 1: Declare External Pin GPIO 15
codeChunks.explanation: Configures physical pin GPIO 15 (labeled D15 on the board) as an electrical output.

codeChunks.title: Step 2: Toggle LED in loop()
codeChunks.explanation: Cycles the external green LED on and off every 500 milliseconds.

verificationChallenge.instruction: Upload the script. The physical green LED standing in your breadboard should blink bright green.
verificationChallenge.expectedObservableResult: A bright green 5mm LED blinking steadily on your breadboard. If it does not light, check whether the long and short legs are reversed.

title: Level 3: Button & Digital Input in C
subtitle: Floating Pins, INPUT_PULLUP Resistors & Decision Trees

conceptByte.title: The 4-Pin Tactile Button & Floating Pins
conceptByte.metaphor: The Helium Balloon & The Floor Anchor
keyTakeaways: Inside a 4-Pin Tactile Button: The button has a square body and 4 metal legs. The legs on the top are permanently connected in pairs, and the legs on the bottom are connected in pairs. Pressing the button connects the top and bottom pairs together!

The Floating Pin Mystery: When an input wire is left unconnected, it acts like an antenna. It picks up stray electrical noise from Wi-Fi, lights, and static, fluctuating wildly between 0 and 1! That is a floating pin.

Internal Pull-Up Resistor (INPUT_PULLUP): The ESP32 chip has internal pull-up resistors on its GPIO pins. Calling pinMode(14, INPUT_PULLUP) gently holds the pin UP to 3.3V (reads HIGH / 1) when released. When you press the button, it connects the pin directly to Ground (0V / LOW).
Active-Low Rule in C: Released = 1 (HIGH), Pressed = 0 (LOW).
conceptByte.analogyStory: An unconnected input pin is like a helium balloon floating in the wind: it blows around randomly. Setting INPUT_PULLUP is like tying that balloon to the ceiling at 3.3V. It stays firmly at 1. When you press the push button, you pull the balloon down to the floor (Ground = 0V). That is why a pressed button reads as 0!

quizGate.question: When a push button is configured with pinMode(14, INPUT_PULLUP) in C, what does digitalRead(14) return when RELEASED?
options: LOW (0 / Ground)
HIGH (1 / 3.3V)
Random fluctuating noise
quizGate.hint: The internal pull-up resistor holds the pin UP to 3.3V until pressed.
quizGate.explanation: When released, the internal pull-up resistor holds the pin steady at 1 (HIGH / 3.3V). Pressing the button connects it to Ground, pulling it down to 0 (LOW).

quizGate.question: Why do engineers use internal pull-up resistors instead of leaving the input pin bare?
options: To prevent the pin from floating and generating false button presses from ambient electromagnetic noise
To make the button louder when clicked
To turn on the Wi-Fi chip
quizGate.hint: A bare wire acts like an antenna and picks up ambient static noise.
quizGate.explanation: A floating pin acts like an antenna. An internal pull-up resistor holds it steady at 3.3V until physically grounded.

circuitSteps.title: Mount 4-Pin Button Across Trench
circuitSteps.instruction: Straddle the 4-pin tactile push button across the center divider trench at Row 10. The legs on the left plug into Column E; the legs on the right plug into Column F.

circuitSteps.title: Wire ESP32 GPIO 14 (D14) to Button
circuitSteps.instruction: Plug a yellow jumper wire from ESP32 D14 (GPIO 14) into Breadboard Row 10, Column D (same row as the left leg of the button).

circuitSteps.title: Wire Button to Ground Rail
circuitSteps.instruction: Plug a black jumper wire from Breadboard Row 10, Column G (right leg of the button) to the Blue Ground Rail (-).

circuitSteps.title: Add Orange Alert LED on GPIO 4 (D4)
circuitSteps.instruction: Insert an Orange LED in Row 20 (long leg in Col C, short leg in GND rail through a 220 ohm resistor). Connect ESP32 D4 (GPIO 4) to Row 20, Col E.

codeChunks.title: Step 1: Declare Button & Dual LEDs in C
codeChunks.explanation: INPUT_PULLUP enables the internal pull-up resistor on GPIO 14, holding it at 3.3V until pressed.

codeChunks.title: Step 2: Active-Low If/Else Decision in loop()
codeChunks.explanation: Reads the pin state with digitalRead(). If LOW (pressed), switches to the Orange alert LED.

verificationChallenge.instruction: Upload code. The green LED should glow. Press and hold the push button; the green LED should turn off and the orange LED should light up instantly.
verificationChallenge.expectedObservableResult: Immediate visual state change between green and orange whenever the push button is held down.

title: Level 4: Drawing on Glass in C
subtitle: Pixels, The I2C Two-Wire Highway & The Framebuffer

conceptByte.title: What is an OLED & How Pixels Work
conceptByte.metaphor: The 8,192 Microscopic Fireflies & The Hidden Sketchpad
keyTakeaways: What is an OLED? OLED stands for Organic Light Emitting Diode. Unlike LCDs that have a big white backlight glowing behind liquid crystal blinds, an OLED display has 8,192 microscopic organic dots that each create their own light! When a pixel is OFF, it emits zero light, giving true pitch black.
What is a Pixel? Pixel = Picture Element. Our 0.96 inch screen has 128 pixels across (X axis: 0 to 127) and 64 pixels down (Y axis: 0 to 63). That is 128 x 64 = 8,192 individual light dots.

The I2C Two-Wire Highway: Controlling 8,192 pixels individually would need thousands of wires. Instead, the I2C protocol uses just 2 wires on ESP32: SDA on GPIO 21 (Serial Data) and SCL on GPIO 22 (Serial Clock, ticking 400,000 times a second).

The Framebuffer Rule in C: The ESP32 prepares the graphic in a 1,024-byte RAM sketchpad called the Framebuffer. Calling display.println() writes text to memory, but nothing appears on screen yet! You MUST call display.display() to blast that memory map down the I2C wires and light up the glass.
conceptByte.analogyStory: Imagine an artist painting behind a thick velvet curtain. Every time you call display.print(), the artist paints words on the canvas in the dark. If you forget to call display.display(), the curtain stays shut and the glass stays black! Calling display.display() pulls open the curtain in one millisecond, revealing your team name in bright glowing pixels.

quizGate.question: What is the difference between an OLED screen and a standard LCD screen?
options: OLED pixels generate their own individual light; LCDs use a constant backlight shining through liquid filters
OLEDs only work in black and white and have no pixels
LCDs are made of paper while OLEDs are made of plastic
quizGate.hint: Organic Light Emitting Diode: every microscopic dot creates its own light.
quizGate.explanation: In an OLED, each individual pixel emits light independently. This allows true deep blacks and high contrast without a bulky backlight.

quizGate.question: Why does nothing appear on the OLED screen until you call display.display() in C?
options: Adafruit GFX draws into an off-screen RAM buffer first; display.display() transmits that image over I2C to the glass
display.display() connects the board to Wi-Fi
The ESP32 needs permission from an operating system
quizGate.hint: Remember the artist painting on the sketchpad behind the closed curtain.
quizGate.explanation: All drawing functions update an off-screen memory buffer (Framebuffer). Calling display.display() pushes the buffer data across the I2C bus to the physical pixels.

circuitSteps.title: Wire OLED SDA to ESP32 D21 (GPIO 21)

circuitSteps.title: Wire OLED SCL to ESP32 D22 (GPIO 22)
circuitSteps.instruction: Connect a yellow jumper wire from ESP32 D22 (GPIO 22) to the OLED SCL pin.

codeChunks.explanation: Imports the Wire (I2C) and Adafruit OLED graphics drivers, configuring the 128x64 display at address 0x3C.

codeChunks.title: Step 2: Personalize Your Team Variables
codeChunks.explanation: Update these character arrays so your team name and school appear on the OLED display.

codeChunks.title: Step 3: Draw on Buffer & Blast to Glass

title: Level 5: The Grand IoT Challenge in C
subtitle: Connecting to the Cloud: ESP32 Wi-Fi, APIs & Closed-Loop Alarms

conceptByte.title: What is an API & The 4 Layers of IoT
keyTakeaways: What is an API? Imagine you are at a restaurant. You cannot walk into the kitchen, open the fridge, and start chopping vegetables yourself! Instead, you look at the menu and give your order to the Waiter. The waiter carries your order to the kitchen and brings back a neat plate of food. An API (Application Programming Interface) is the digital waiter! Your ESP32 sends a polite HTTP GET request: 'Hey API, give me the latest temperature!' The API fetches the data and hands it back in a neat JSON box.
Layer 1 (Perception): Physical sensors touching nature (temperature probes, humidity chips, soil moisture sensors in dirt).
Layer 2 (Network): ESP32 Wi-Fi radio waves transmitting data packets through the air to the internet router.
Layer 3 (Cloud Data): The central server (ThingSpeak or classroom server) recording and organizing sensor numbers 24/7.
Layer 4 (Application): Your team's OLED display and warning buzzer automatically alerting you when soil dries out or temperatures spike.
conceptByte.analogyStory: When the teacher dips a soil probe into water at the front of the classroom, that measurement climbs a 4-story tower: from wet soil (Layer 1), through invisible Wi-Fi airwaves (Layer 2), into the central cloud database (Layer 3), and down to your team's OLED screen (Layer 4). Your ESP32 acts like a customer ordering fresh numbers from the API waiter every 15 seconds!

quizGate.question: In the restaurant analogy, why is an API compared to a waiter?
options: It takes your program's request, communicates with the central server/database, and delivers the data back safely
It serves drinks to the computer chips
It cleans up memory when the computer turns off
quizGate.hint: An API is a safe messenger between your code and an external server.
quizGate.explanation: An API acts like a waiter: your code asks for specific data, the API queries the database, and returns the response in a standardized format.

quizGate.question: Which of the 4 layers of IoT does your team's OLED screen and alarm buzzer belong to?
options: Layer 1: Perception Layer (Raw sensors in soil)
Layer 2: Network Layer (Wi-Fi radio waves)
Layer 4: Application Layer (Dashboards, screens, and automated alerts)
quizGate.hint: The Application Layer is where humans see data and actuators take physical action.
quizGate.explanation: OLED screens, mobile dashboards, and warning buzzers belong to Layer 4 (Application Layer).

circuitSteps.title: Wire Active Buzzer to ESP32 D19 (GPIO 19)
circuitSteps.instruction: Plug the Active Buzzer Signal pin into ESP32 D19 (GPIO 19). Connect Buzzer VCC to the 3.3V rail and GND to the ground rail.

circuitSteps.title: Wire Red Alert LED to ESP32 D18 (GPIO 18)
circuitSteps.instruction: Connect Red LED Anode to ESP32 D18 (GPIO 18) through a 220 ohm resistor and Cathode to the Ground rail.

codeChunks.title: Step 2: HTTP GET from API & Parse JSON

verificationChallenge.instruction: Watch your OLED screen synchronize with the live classroom feed. When the facilitator triggers a temperature or soil spike in the dashboard, verify your OLED and buzzer react within 15 seconds.
verificationChallenge.expectedObservableResult: All team OLED screens and warning buzzers trigger in unison based on broadcast sensor changes.
